title: Northern Ireland’s budget crisis and the challenge of rebuilding confidence
label: 18 November 2026 · Northern Ireland Secretary hearing
summary: The committee questioned the Secretary of State and his team about Northern Ireland’s unresolved budget, the risk to public services, and possible changes to political arrangements. They also discussed community tensions after Drumcree, the future of investigations into Troubles-era deaths, policing, energy support and the effects of trade rules. The Secretary of State said the Executive must make difficult spending and revenue decisions, but warned that the UK Government may have to intervene if services are at risk. Members pressed him to act sooner and to ensure that victims, families and businesses receive practical answers.

glossary.definition: Northern Ireland’s devolved government, made up of ministers from its political parties.
Extra funding for devolved governments when UK Government spending changes elsewhere.

The Independent Commission for Reconciliation and Information Recovery, set up to investigate Troubles-related deaths and serious harm.

chapters.title: The budget impasse
chapters.takeaway: The Secretary of State said the Executive must live within the funding offered, while warning that a prolonged failure to agree a budget could disrupt services.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What’s the latest on budget talks with the parties in the Executive?

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: There’s been no progress. Parties keep asking for more money, but our offer is final. The Executive is legally responsible for setting its budget, and it has to make the sums add up.

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: Our offer includes an extra £500 million a year for three years, on top of other funding. That would bring Northern Ireland’s spending per person to about 126% of England’s, above the 124% level used as a fair-funding guide.

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: The parties’ requests keep changing; one recent figure was £1.5 billion for this year. They also need to consider raising revenue. For example, household rates and water charges are much lower in Northern Ireland than in several English and Scottish areas.

turns.speaker: Robin Swann
turns.text: The frustration is shared here. Health workers still haven’t received their pay award, and doctors are preparing to strike. But the ministers responsible can’t approve the award without an agreed budget.

turns.speaker: Robin Swann
turns.text: Previous Secretaries of State have stepped in when the Executive couldn’t set a budget. If this deadlock continues, when will you do that?

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: I don’t have a plan to impose a budget today, and it would be unusual for the UK Government to do so. But I won’t avoid my responsibilities if there’s no other choice.

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: The Executive can currently spend up to 95% of last year’s budget while waiting for a new one. That lawful spending could run out around the end of January. Schools and hospitals would probably stay open, but other work could be stopped or delayed.

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: If there’s no budget before the financial year ends, they can’t spend next year, even money they raise themselves. Departments and community organisations have no certainty about next year’s funding.

turns.speaker: Sarah Owen
turns.text: Businesses tell me they couldn’t go months without setting a budget or making difficult choices. The uncertainty puts off investment and affects the whole economy, not just public services.

turns.speaker: Simon Hoare
turns.text: You’ve described the harm clearly. What exactly would make you say, ‘Now I have to set a budget’? Is there a date or a specific event?

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: We’re close to a point where we may have no choice. But most of the financial information is held by the Executive, and we’ve only just received more of the figures we requested.

turns.speaker: Sorcha Eastwood
turns.text: Is the additional money conditional on the Executive raising revenue?

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: Yes. The offer expects it to raise £100 million next year and £200 million the year after. Those are small sums compared with the overall budget. The aim is to put the finances on a stable footing over three years.

turns.speaker: Sorcha Eastwood
turns.text: Would an interim budget that runs into the election period be lawful if it doesn’t balance?

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: The budget has to balance. Pay awards were predictable, so the Executive should have planned for them rather than discovering late in the year that it couldn’t afford them.

turns.speaker: Claire Hanna
turns.text: Are you still considering urgent changes before the election to make it harder to stop the Assembly working or bring down the Executive?

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: Yes, but we haven’t settled what those changes should be. The immediate priority is financial accountability. I don’t want to take powers away from the Executive, but we may have to decide what happens if services are put at risk.

chapters.title: Political reform and community relations
chapters.takeaway: Members called for changes to prevent political stand-offs, while ministers said trust after Drumcree will take sustained work and a fair review of parade decisions.

turns.speaker: Sir Alec Shelbrooke
turns.text: Could public pressure help you act? People may support intervention if they understand what will happen when there’s no budget.

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: People I meet feel let down by politicians, but public opinion is hard to measure. I believe in devolution and don’t want to take powers away, though I would if that became necessary.

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: I’m also frustrated by Northern Ireland’s missed opportunities. It has strong businesses, creative industries and expertise in areas such as cyber-security and defence. Its access to both the UK and EU markets could be an advantage.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What are you doing to repair community relations in Portadown after the events around Drumcree?

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: We brought the parties together and came close to an agreement, but it fell apart. The important thing is that people turned to the courts rather than violence. Most of Northern Ireland’s roughly 4,000 annual parades take place without dispute.

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: We asked Justice O’Hara to review the Parades Commission, and expect his report shortly. We’ll appoint new commissioners soon. I wanted some time to pass before starting wider talks about community relations.

turns.speaker: Baroness Anderson
turns.text: The hurt was real across communities, and the peace process remains fragile. Some people have lived separately from other parts of their town for decades. Rebuilding trust will take time and must respect different experiences and identities.

turns.speaker: Baroness Anderson
turns.text: We need to make sure people on both sides have confidence in the Parades Commission. Some local agreements, such as those around parades in Derry/Londonderry, show that culture can be celebrated without making others feel threatened.

turns.speaker: Sir Alec Shelbrooke
turns.text: Why did you prohibit the Orange Order parade on 9 October? And how do you stop people concluding that whoever makes the biggest fuss gets their way next year?

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: We first tried to reach a negotiated settlement and waited as long as we could before using powers that had never been used before. The Chief Constable asked me to act, but I used a different legal power. The decision was upheld through the courts.

turns.speaker: Baroness Anderson
turns.text: The review should help clarify what the Commission is expected to do. We’ll use it as we appoint new members, while trying to preserve the confidence people already have and build confidence where it’s lacking.

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: The goal should be respect, not simply putting up with other communities. We won’t always get everyone to agree, but we should seek the widest possible agreement.

chapters.title: Investigations, victims and reconciliation
chapters.takeaway: The ministers said the new legacy body must give families meaningful answers, while members challenged delays, funding and whether reconciliation is being clearly defined.

turns.speaker: Mike Kane
turns.text: What’s stopping you from naming Freddie Scappaticci as Stakeknife, the British agent within the IRA?

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: I haven’t progressed the question yet. I need to meet Sir Iain Livingstone and speak with others in Government. A civil case is still under way, and the Government has long followed a policy of neither confirming nor denying intelligence identities.

turns.speaker: Mike Kane
turns.text: Families are still grieving and need answers. Will you return to Parliament once you’ve reached a decision?

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: Yes. Once I’ve reached a settled position, I’ll explain it to the House.

turns.speaker: Simon Hoare
turns.text: Victims and survivors have been frustrated by the tone of debate on the Troubles Bill. How will you make sure they stay at its centre?

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: The debate has focused heavily on veterans’ concerns, which I understand, but this legislation is primarily about families getting answers. The new Legacy Commission must be able to do that job.

turns.speaker: Baroness Anderson
turns.text: The bill is due to have its next major debate in the House of Lords on 2 December. I’ve promised victims’ groups that I’ll refer to victims in every speech I make.

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: I want the Irish Government’s legislation to move in step with ours, so the two systems can work together. I also think it should drop its legal case against the UK, because I can’t see a reason for continuing it.

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: The UK inquiry into the Omagh bombing is independent, and it must reach its own conclusions. I think it’s very likely that the Republic of Ireland will eventually need its own inquiry too, though it has said not yet.

turns.speaker: Baroness Anderson
turns.text: The new commission is meant to begin work within four months of the bill becoming law. We’re working to ensure it’s ready. Most recommendations from the Peter May review have been dealt with, and the bill includes changes to improve its oversight and culture.

turns.speaker: Simon Hoare
turns.text: The commission has requested £628 million over ten years. Will it have enough funding to begin properly?

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: We’re making the case to the Treasury. We’re also working with the commission on ways to save money without making it harder to give families answers.

turns.speaker: Julie Harrison
turns.text: Reports need security checks, which involve the police and others. We may disagree about the order of the steps, but we’ll work to complete them as quickly as we can.

turns.speaker: Julie Harrison
turns.text: We’re also talking with the commission about how families experience investigations. Some want to speak directly with investigators rather than feel that support staff are standing between them and the person handling their case.

turns.speaker: Robin Swann
turns.text: The Irish authorities still haven’t provided the information the commission needs. Can you point to information they’ve shared without being forced through legal action?

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: The commission hasn’t received all the information it wants, and I’ve raised that with the Irish Government. Their laws need to change, and I hope cooperation will improve as both countries pass their legislation.

turns.speaker: Mr Kohler
turns.text: Some families value answers even without prosecutions. Could the bill put more emphasis on restorative justice and define how progress on reconciliation will be measured?

turns.speaker: Baroness Anderson
turns.text: You can’t legislate a single definition of reconciliation that every community will accept. Families want different things: some want responsibility acknowledged, some want answers, and some want prosecutions. The process has to respond to those differences.

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: The commission itself can help people get answers, but we shouldn’t promise that it will resolve every case or bring families face to face with those responsible. We can seek broad agreement, but not unanimity.

chapters.title: Policing and the legacy of violence
chapters.takeaway: Ministers praised the PSNI’s progress but said intimidation and organised crime still make community policing difficult.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What are you doing about paramilitary groups, and are you concerned about the resources available to local police?

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: We received a report on how paramilitary groups might move towards disbanding only a few weeks ago. I’ll discuss it with my Irish counterpart and hope to bring forward proposals. The goal is for all terrorist groups to give up weapons and return to democratic politics.

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: Policing is devolved, but Northern Ireland’s police face additional costs. A more stable political and security situation could help free resources for officers. Recruitment must also reflect all communities.

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: Former terrorists, current terrorists and organised crime can be closely linked. Intimidation can control a community even without bombs, and sometimes makes it harder for police to investigate.

turns.speaker: Sarah Owen
turns.text: I visited the police training college and met new recruits from different communities. Their enthusiasm was encouraging, but the police also need to tackle issues such as violence against women and girls.

turns.speaker: Baroness Anderson
turns.text: Police officers in Northern Ireland work under a particular threat. Their bravery is often celebrated in private because of the security risks. We should recognise what they do and the conditions they face.

chapters.title: Household costs, business and trade
chapters.takeaway: The Government pointed to some cost-of-living help and planned business advice, while members pressed for clearer timelines and support for Northern Ireland firms.

turns.speaker: Claire Hanna
turns.text: Can households in Northern Ireland receive the £100 energy payment announced in the UK Budget?

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: The Executive would need a budget before it could spend that money. Northern Ireland households should also benefit from removing a tax on heating oil, which is used by about 68% of homes, and we hope to extend a VAT cut from next April.

turns.speaker: Sarah Owen
turns.text: The Budget also extended a fuel-duty cut that reduces the cost of red diesel for rural and farming communities through June and July 2027.

turns.speaker: Robin Swann
turns.text: When will Northern Ireland businesses receive support comparable to the UK scheme for industries with high electricity costs?

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: We haven’t settled the figure because energy works differently in Northern Ireland. I’ll write to the committee when we have an answer.

turns.speaker: Robin Swann
turns.text: Will the planned closer relationship with the EU change whether Northern Ireland businesses can use that UK support?

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: I don’t think it will, but I’ll check. A closer EU relationship could reduce paperwork and checks for trade, especially for farmers and businesses moving goods.

turns.speaker: Sarah Owen
turns.text: We’re setting up a one-stop service so businesses can find advice, support and answers in one place.

turns.speaker: Fleur Johnson
turns.text: It’ll be online, with an AI tool for straightforward questions and a call centre for people who need more help. We’re testing an early version at the end of this year and expect the full service by the end of the financial year.

turns.speaker: Robin Swann
turns.text: Businesses have heard promises about help before. The Windsor Framework monitoring panel is also overdue to report. People need delivery, not another promise of something coming soon.

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: I agree that things need to move faster. I’ve read the panel’s draft report, which is encouraging about how trade is working, but Northern Ireland also needs to make the most of its economic opportunities.

turns.speaker: Fleur Johnson
turns.text: We’ve met hauliers and set up a working group with them and the EU to address problems with customs processes. We’re looking at what can be made simpler within the Windsor Framework.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The committee has heard that some firms in Great Britain have stopped selling to Northern Ireland. Are you considering the trusted-haulier proposal?

turns.speaker: Fleur Johnson
turns.text: We’re working directly with hauliers on practical improvements and on whether closer work with the EU can make shipments more flexible.

turns.speaker: Chris Bryant
turns.text: We’ve also secured £1 million for a trade and investment summit next year, to promote Northern Ireland’s businesses at home and abroad.
